notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2001.tlg041.1st1K-gr: 1.1: Aristotle's work is cited as 'On Sense and Sensibles'. 1.2: in 'πρὸς τὸν καὶ πολυτίμητον νοῦν' an adjective seems to have dropped out; '[divine]' is supplied as a conjecture. Near the end of 1.2 the text reads 'λήψεται' ('it will take it as a span or a cubit'), but the sense requires a negative; the line is translated as 'it will not take it'. 1.4: Antipheron of Oreus is the man Aristotle mentions as taking his images for memories. Many obvious scanning errors (e.g. ρ for φ, κ for χ, doubled words) were silently corrected.

In 1.5, 'τόπων' ('places') may be a misreading of 'τύπων' ('impressions'); 'places' is kept to match the later discussion of τόποι. Several scanning errors are corrected silently, e.g. ἠράνισται for ἠφάνισται and Κοπίσκου for Κορίσκου. In 1.6, πλευρώνη is uncertain: it is apparently a name derived from πλευρά ('rib'), perhaps the town Pleuron, and is rendered 'Pleurone'. The following stretch has πλευρωνία. The quotation 'In place of much wealth, men of Athens...' is the opening of Demosthenes, First Olynthiac. The '|' marks in the text are page breaks and are left out. In 'γινομένων κινήσεων ἔπεται' the sense is somewhat compressed. 'Λύκιον' is taken as the Lyceum.

In 1.7 πλευρωνία is rendered 'Pleurone' after the glossary; its sense (a place-name, or a coinage on πλευρά set against πλευρῖτις) is uncertain. In the diagram ΘΣ (1.8) appears where ΘΞ is expected; probably a misprint. In 1.8 ἐμβεβληένου and in 1.10 ἤρεκσε, ἀνμνησθῆναι, μνηονεύειν are read as scanning errors. In 1.10 'ἀναγνῶναι γνῶναι' looks like a dittography; translated as 'to read'. 'κρίναντος τοῦ λογισμοῦ' is odd; translated literally ('after reason has judged'). 'ἀμμένειν' read as ἀναμένειν/ἐμμένειν, 'retain'.

The heading reads ΕΡΡΗΡΟΡΣΩΣ, a scanning error for ἐγρηγόρσεως. In 2.3 'ἐν τῷ καλουμένῳ' appears to lack a noun (ὕπνῳ, 'sleep') and has been supplied in brackets; 'μή, μή, τῇ ὄψει' is read as 'μή, οἷον τῇ ὄψει'. Parentheses in 2.3 are unbalanced in the printed text; the sense has been followed.

In 2.4 the parenthesis is unclosed in the text; read as closing after 'καὶ οὐ καθεύδειν τοῦτο' (so translated). In 2.6 'ἐγγίνεται δὲ αὐτῷ ἡ αἰσθητικὴ ὑστέρα ἀποτεκθέντι' is odd (perhaps 'ὕστερον'); rendered 'later, after it is born'. Numerous scanning errors and duplicated syllables corrected silently.

2.7: αἶραι taken as 'darnel'. 'κατάπτυξιν' read as κατάψυξιν ('cooling'). 'ὅταν καὶ δέῃ τοῦτο παθεῖν' rendered 'whenever they are bound to suffer it'; sense uncertain. 2.8: 'καὶ γὰρ αἱ κοιλίαι γὰρ θερμότητος' is corrupt; a verb such as δέονται ('need') is supplied, and κοιλίαι is taken as 'passages'. 'οὐδ’ ἀπολελαυκότα' is obscure; rendered 'as if they had not benefited [from food]'. 2.9: 'τοῖς δὲ μὴ ἔχουσι τὸ ἀνάλογον τούτου μόριον' is elliptical; the sense supplied is that in animals without a brain the analogous part is coldest. The subject of 'ἐπιπεσὼν' is taken to be the heat.

Many scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. συνεεωσμένη for συνεωσμένη, ὀλίγῳ, θλολώτερον, συγκατατιξέμεθα κατατιξέμεθα and other duplications). In 3.2 the sentence 'when someone sees something and does not think...' is somewhat garbled in the text (ὄναρ ἐνύπνιον τοῦτό γε; ὅοκεῖ for ὅτι); translated by evident sense. 'Can grasp that we are awake' (ἐγρηγόραμεν) in 3.5 seems to require 'that we are asleep' in sense; translated as printed. The first-person anecdotes about the book and the 'most revered master' are Sophonias' own additions. In 3.3 εἰδόσιν εἰσόσιν is a dittography.

3.6: δύσοσμοι τῶν ὁμοίων is compressed; rendered 'poor at smelling similar [smells]'. 3.8: ἀδήποτε read as ὁτιδήποτε ('anything whatever'). 3.9: ἐγρηγόρως read as ἐγρηγορότως ('as though awake'); ρως ἀντέχεται read as ἐρρωμένως ('strongly'). The sentence 'so that if the one thing ... altogether believed' is corrupt (φανττατως, probably φαίνεται, with something lost); rendered by sense. In the frogs passage 'in the motion that entered first, this one which will be active after it comes to the surface' follows the Greek, which is awkward and may be corrupt. ἀνιμένου is read as ἀνιεμένου ('relaxed').

In 3.10 'μνημονεύειν' is taken as 'remember'. In 4.1 'κατὰ τοὺς πολλάκις' read as 'τοῖς πολλοῖς πολλάκις'. The parenthesis in 3.10 ('ἧ γὰρ ἄν ἐμνημόνευον') is left unclosed in the edition. Many OCR errors corrected silently.

Several scanning errors read silently (e.g. χρόνοις for κρόνοις). εὐλόχων read as εὐλόγχων ('fortunate', Democritus' prayer). Θιλαιγίδου read as Φιλαιγίδου (Philaegides, as in Aristotle De div. 464b); 'μεταΜὰ:' after ἔχοντα is printer's debris and omitted. The clause about melancholics (διὰ τὸ σφοδρὸν τοξευθέν, ὅσα καὶ χειρί…) seems corrupt; translated after Aristotle's comparison with long-distance archers. 'Each… interpreter' (ἑκάτερος) is rendered as two parallel figures, the interpreter of reflections and of dreams.

nodes.text: Paraphrase of the books On Memory and Recollection, and of the books that follow these, of Aristotle, by the most wise lord Sophonias

Concerning memory and remembering, we must say what it is, through what cause it comes about, and to which of the parts of the soul this affection belongs, and recollecting too. For the same people are not good at remembering and good at recollecting. Rather, for the most part, slow people are better at remembering, while quick people who learn easily are better at recollecting. The objects of activities are clearer than the activities, and so in On Sense and Sensibles we first made our account from the underlying objects, as being more evident. In the same way here too we must first consider what sorts of things are objects of memory, for people are often deceived about this. It is not possible to remember the future: that is an object of opinion and of expectation (there might even be a science of expectation, as some say divination is). Nor is it possible to remember the present: of the present there is perception. By perception we know neither the future nor what has happened, but only the present. It remains, then, that it is the past that is remembered, and memory is of what has happened. No one would say that he remembers the present while it is present, for example this white thing while he sees it. Nor does someone contemplating an object of contemplation and thought remember it while he is just now contemplating and thinking it for the first time. Rather, people say that in the one case he perceives, and in the other that he learns and is brought to knowledge. But suppose someone has the knowledge and the perception without the actual objects (by objects I mean, for example, this animal, or this white thing, or the triangle in this book), and also thinks of the time besides. Then he would be said to remember simply. Thus he remembers of the angles of the triangle that they are equal to two right angles, and of Socrates that he is white. In the first case it is because he once learned it from this person in this place, or contemplated it; in the second it is because he heard or saw it, or something of the sort. For whenever the soul is active in remembering, it is also aware of time. (Remembering is contemplating the impressions of the things in the soul, not in themselves but as images of other things.) For so the soul says: that it perceived or thought this before. Memory, then, is neither perception nor imagination nor any other kind of thought. It is a state or affection of one of these, when time is taken in besides: the time in which the residue came about, and from which it dates. But the activity in the present of what is now active is not memory, as has been said. For there is perception of the present, expectation of the future, and memory of what has happened. Hence all memory involves time. Therefore only those animals which perceive time remember, and they remember with no other part of the soul than the one with which they perceive. For the donkey that fell into this pit last year, seeing it today and drawing back, remembers that it fell before. There is, however, a difference. A human being, besides being aware of when he saw or heard, also knows the difference of the past from the future, while irrational animals know only that they are falling now or fell long ago. And the human is aware of himself as remembering, while they are not. Further, among the irrational animals, those with a purer imagination are also better at remembering, such as the bee and the dove and the like, while those with a confused imagination, such as flies and worms, lack memory.

But someone might raise a difficulty. If we remember with the same faculty with which we also perceive, there would be no memory of intelligibles. But there is such memory, for we remember theorems, and the intellect dwells on the more universal of these above all. If so, it remains to say that remembering belongs not to the perceptive soul alone but also to the rational soul. Or is it rather that memory is of perceptibles in itself, as imagination also is, but of intelligibles incidentally? For the intellect is interwoven with imagination, and from the impressions inscribed in imagination by actual perception it strips off the universals. Just as there is no imagination without actual perception, so there is no grasping of the universal apart from imagination. If this is so, it is clear what follows. Perception sees in itself the elephant painted at Athens, but incidentally the one grazing in India. Or again, when we see this Socrates here, we think besides of the common and specific human being. In the same way memory is active in itself about the impressions and residues in imagination, but incidentally about universals. So memory belongs in itself to the primary perceptive faculty, to which imagination also belongs, and incidentally to what is thought. For the same thing happens in thinking as in drawing a diagram. In drawing, we make no use of the triangle's being of a definite size, and yet we draw it definite in size. (In the demonstration that the three angles of a triangle are equal to two right angles, we need no definite size for the demonstration. Whether each of the sides is supposed a finger long, or a span long, or any length whatever, they will be shown to be equal to two right angles. Yet we draw a definite triangle, for whatever is drawn must be equilateral or something of the sort, and every rectilinear figure that is drawn is definite.) The one who thinks is in the same case. Even if he is not thinking of a quantity but of some other category, he still thinks it together with a quantity. For whether he thinks of something hot, or a smell, or something white, or any other of the things without parts, he nevertheless sets a quantity before his eyes: either a white surface or a hot body. Indeed, even if he ever turns to the [divine] and most honoured intellect, he at once imagines some bulks and extensions there too. And what Plato says about imagination is true: that, being joined to the thoughts of the intellect, it does not allow them to be made pure. Perhaps, however, even if it thinks of things without quantity and without body together with quantity, it does not think of them as quantities. It thinks of white as what dilates sight and black as what contracts it. And even if the object of thought is of the nature of quantities, such as a triangle or a square, that too is indefinite and not of such and such a magnitude. It will not take it as perhaps a span or a cubit long, nor as scalene or equilateral, but simply a triangle. The form, and the account of the triangle in the universal, are without extension, but the impression in the imagination is in a way composite and is bounded by magnitude: as large as the thing lying outside was, so large is it imagined within. So we think nothing without an image; imagination is always present with thought, either helping or hindering it: helping, as in mathematics (for there it serves the intellect as a kind of drawing-board), but hindering the contemplation of intelligible and divine things by bringing in shapes, magnitudes and colours. And this is the reason why eternal things cannot be thought without the continuous, nor things in time without time.

If, then, all the things from which the intellect strips off the universal are objects of imagination, and imagination and memory are the same in their substrate (for both are affections of the common sense), it is at once clear that memory and imagination are of intelligibles only incidentally. It is also clear that knowledge of these, and surely of time and motion too, belongs to the primary perceptive faculty. That is why memory belongs to some other animals as well, and not only to human beings and to those that have opinion and practical wisdom. If it belonged to one of the intellective parts and to the rational soul, it would not belong to many of the animals, and perhaps to none of the irrational ones. As it is, it does not belong to all of them either, because not all have perception of time. For whenever one is active with memory, as we said before as well, one perceives besides that one saw, or heard, or learned, or experienced this before; and before and after are in time. To which of the parts of the soul memory belongs is therefore evident: to the same part as imagination. The things of which there is imagination are objects of memory in themselves; those that do not occur without imagination are objects of memory incidentally.

Someone might raise this difficulty. Only the affection, the residue, is present in imagination, and the thing itself is absent. How then does one remember what is not present? For memory is of the thing, not of the impression. So that we may reach a solution more easily, and so that both what has been said and what follows may become clear, let us first set out from the beginning a little of what concerns imagination. It was discussed in On the Soul too. Nonetheless, for the present need we must understand this. From our activities about perceptibles there comes to be in us a kind of impression or painted likeness in the primary perceptive organ, which is the heart, as with people sealing with signet rings. Such a residue, which remains even when the perceptible is not present, they call imagination; that is why they also define it as an impression in the ruling part. But perhaps imagination is not the impression itself, but the activity of the imaginative faculty about the impression. Otherwise we would be in a state of imagination even when not active about the impression, simply by having it. And we would be in many imaginings at once, as many as the impressions we preserve. Further, by imagination they mean either the image now coming to be and being impressed, or the one that has already come to be and exists. If they mean the one coming to be, they would be describing perception in act. If they mean the one that has come to be and is preserved, they would be describing memory. But consider the case of perception. There one thing is the perceptible, another the perceptive faculty, and a third the perception, that is, the faculty's activity about the perceptible. In the case of thinking, too, one thing is the intelligible, another the intellect, another the act of thinking. We must suppose that it is the same with imagination: one thing is the imaginative faculty, another the object of imagination, another the imagining. The activity of the perceptive faculty that comes about when the perceptible is present is perception. In the same way, the activity that comes about, when the perceptible is not present, in the impression and the residue is imagination. With imagination, we must take 'impression' in a more general sense. Strictly, an impression is one made by indentation and projection, or the shape of what makes the impression arising in what receives it, as we see with seals. But the residues of perceptibles do not come to be in us in that way. For the apprehension of these did not take place by shape in the first place: what shape has white, or colour at all, or smell? So here we use 'impression' rather loosely, for lack of a more proper term. What imagination is has now been said; memory is its persistence and preservation. With this laid down, the following holds. We imprint the impressions of things on the primary sense organ, as has been said. In some this organ is moister and in others harder, and in some it is in motion and in others not. Necessarily, then, the impressions are engraved in some and not in others, and in some they remain for a long time, in others for a short time. Hence some people remember more, some less, and some very little. The organ is in motion in the very young and in the very old, for in the one it is growing and in the other wasting; in some it is also moved through disease. It is not in motion in those who are of middle age and temperament. A seal from a ring would not be imprinted in flowing water. Just so, memory does not arise in those whose sense organ is in motion through age or disease. Nor does it arise in those whose organ is too hard, just as no seal would take in stone. That is why the very young and the old have poor memories: the former are in flux through growth, the latter through wasting. In old people the heart, the primary perceptive organ, is like old buildings. It crumbles as it cools and wipes out the impressions of things in it, as old buildings shed the plaster smeared on them and the figures painted on them. Likewise, those who are very quick and those who are very slow are both seen to have poor memories. The former are moister than they should be, the latter harder. In the former the image does not remain in the soul; the latter it does not take hold of at all. Having taken in these points from outside for the sake of clarity, we set out again the difficulty raised at the beginning, for we are now readier for its solution than before. If, then, this is what happens in memory, does the soul remember this affection, or that from which it came? If this, we would remember none of the absent things. If that, how is it that while perceiving this we remember what we do not perceive? Further, suppose the impression or painting in us is something like the thing, and the perception is of this impression itself. Whether it is like or unlike, why would there be memory of something else and not of this itself? For the one who is active with memory contemplates this affection and perceives it. How then does he remember what is not present? For then it would also be possible to see and to hear what is not present. Or is there a way in which this is possible and does happen? A figure painted on a panel is both a figure and an image: one in substrate, different in account. So it is here too. In that case, when someone looks at the figure on the panel as a thing in itself, simply admiring or faulting the craftsmanship and not thinking besides that it is a likeness of something else, it is called simply a figure. But when, besides seeing it, he refers it and reckons besides that it is a likeness of this real animal, it is called an image. In the same way we must suppose that the image in us is both something in itself and a residue of something else. Insofar as it is something in itself, it is an object of contemplation or an image; insofar as it is of something else, like a likeness, it is a memento. When the common sense is active about the impression in the heart as itself, this is called an object of contemplation, as has been said, or an image. When, while active, it perceives besides that it is of something else, then this is a likeness and a memento, and such an activity of the soul is memory. That is why sometimes we do not know whether what we have through memory arose through perceiving. For often, as the thoughts of the soul unfold, we imagine some things whose time or place, or the person from whom we took them, we do not know. Then we dispute whether we ourselves are the discoverers of the thought or its learners, and whether this is simply imagination or memory. For example, I once heard an argument from someone; later I think of the argument but do not recall from whom I heard it. So I say in perplexity: am I myself now the father of this argument, or where do I have it from? And I waver. When I recall that I have the argument from elsewhere, it then becomes memory, whereas before it was a thought. Sometimes the opposite also happens, as happened to Antipheron of Oreus and to others who were out of their minds. They spoke of their images as things that had happened, and as though they were remembering them. Others, again, speak of their perceptions as images, and others the reverse. This happens when someone contemplates what is not a likeness as a likeness, or the likeness as not a likeness. Exercises preserve memory by reminding us again, and this is nothing other than contemplating something often as a likeness and not as a thing in itself. It has now been said what memory and remembering are: a state of an image, when that image is of something that has lasted for a time after it came to be. And it has been said to which of the parts in us it belongs: to the primary perceptive faculty, the one by which we perceive time.

It remains to speak about recollecting. First, then, we must take as true and established what has been shown in our dialectical and problem-posing discussions. These are that recollection is neither the recovery of memory nor its acquisition. For we do not say that someone recollects who is now learning and acquiring for the first time what he never acquired or learned before; rather, he is learning. Nor do we say it of someone who has learned and keeps the memory, with no forgetting having intervened at all. We say it of someone who previously held the whole intact, later lost part and kept part, and recovers the rest from what was kept. For it is like this. When the whole impression, the re-painting that arises in the primary sense organ from perception in actuality, remains and is preserved so distinct, bright and clean that it can move the soul as a whole, and can be seen by the soul as a whole and put forward as a likeness of something, this is memory, about which we have spoken. But when some part of the whole remains and some part has vanished, through time or some other mishap, so that it neither moves the soul nor is the soul moved by it, and then from the part left behind, which is distinct and clean, what is continuous with the clean part (this was the faint and wholly darkened part) is moved with motions, and is, as it were, unravelled and found by the soul, this is recollection. It is, as it were, a re-painting of the former memory, not of the whole of it (for that is learning) but of a part. When we recover the whole, having evidently lost it, that is learning; for it is possible to learn and to discover the same thing twice. For example, from hearing or seeing in actuality an impression has come to be in the soul of "Sing, goddess, the wrath of Achilles son of Peleus". If this impression remains entire, strong and clean, so that we can recite it whole without hindrance and put it forward whole, this is memory. But if "Sing, goddess, the wrath" remains, while what follows has dropped away through time and forgetting, and then the soul, moved from what remains by certain similar or dissimilar places, finds what is missing as well, this is recollection. And it is clear from this that there is no recollection of simple names, but either memory or learning, unless, as often happens with these too, the first syllable remains and we discover the rest in addition. Memory follows recollection of necessity: for one who has recollected has in a way remembered, since he makes a recovery of part of the former memory. And recollection must differ from learning and discovery in that those who recollect have in them a greater starting point than that from which people learn, since all teaching and all intellectual learning comes about from pre-existing knowledge. What recollection is, then, has been said: a renewal of memory. Where it comes from is clear. Since one motion in the soul naturally follows another, if it does so of necessity, it is clear that when the soul is moved with the first it will be moved with the second; if not of necessity but by habit, it will be moved so for the most part. For just as in a chain, when this link is raised, the next is moved of necessity, and through it the one after, so it is with the impressions in the soul: once the soul has been moved by one of them, at once the next moves it too, and the one after that. For example, Coriscus was a musician who had a lyre, and an impression both of the lyre and of Coriscus came to be in the soul. After this I saw Socrates, let us say, holding a lyre, and at once I recollected the lyre of Coriscus, and then Coriscus. Again, I heard someone singing, "Two souls were going out, and one said to the other, where must we go?" Some time later I heard another singing a melody in that same rhythm but with different words, such as "The first intellect leads me, and again carries me down", and, moved by the melody alone, I came to recollect the first words, "Two souls were going out", and the singer.

This being so, there are some impressions that follow one another of necessity. For one who has remembered fire must think of heat along with it, and one who was struck by Socrates must, on recollecting Socrates, also recollect that he was struck by him in such and such a place. But where it is not of necessity but by habit, the second things do not always follow the first, but only for the most part. What is meant will be clear as follows. Often, when I wanted to say "Lycabettus", I could not recollect it, so I accustomed myself to think of a wolf (for both begin with the syllable "ly"); and setting out from the wolf I would recollect Lycabettus. Someone else, forgetting "Tauromenite", accustomed himself to go at once to the thought of a bull; and another, by habit, recovered "Pleurone" from "rib" [pleura]. In these cases, at any rate, the rest does not always follow the first; often I think of the rib but do not recollect Pleurone. It happens that some people are habituated more by one occurrence than others are by being moved many times. That is why some remember certain things seen once better than others seen many times. When we recollect, then, we are moved with some of the prior and leading motions, until we are moved with the one after which that motion habitually comes. That is why we hunt for what comes next, starting our thought from the present or from something else; and for this reason recollection also comes about from what is similar, or opposite, or close by. For the motions of some of these are the same, of others simultaneous, and others share a part. For example, someone saw a painted lyre and, moved by it as prior and leading, recollected a lyre, from this the musician, and from him the song he sang. Often it comes from something else too: if the impression of a column happens to be next to the impression of the song, I will recollect the song from the column. From the similar and the opposite: when from a portrait of Socrates I recollect Socrates, from black white, and from heat cold. From what is close by: when from "In place of much wealth, men of Athens" I recollect "I think you would choose what benefits the city". The beginning, then, is the greatest part of everything, and once it is found what comes after it is small; so when the beginning is grasped, what follows is strung together. If sometimes, even when it has been found and the first part has been moved, what lies on either side does not follow, one should not be surprised: when something has been completely obliterated, it will not follow. When people search, then, recollection comes about in this way, from the things we mentioned: from similar things, or opposed ones, or near ones. But when it happens to people who are not searching to recollect, it comes from none of these. For when someone, having remembered a song, recollects Socrates, he has made the recollection neither from something similar nor from opposites or near things. But this is rare and seldom; for most things follow as other motions occur. Those who treat of recollection need not examine how we recollect distant and old things, but near things and what we perceived or were taught a little before; for these, because of their nearness, serve teaching better than those. | Yet the manner of recollecting both is one and the same. For just as with near things someone, searching from the starting point within him, strings together and recollects what follows (for the motions follow by habit, as has been said, one after another), so also when someone recollects things of which he acquired knowledge long ago. For there too he will seek to take hold of a starting point of motion, after which that motion will come. That is why recollections come about fastest and best from the beginning. For as things stand to one another in sequence, so do the motions; and things that have some order, a first and a second, are easy to remember, such as mathematical subjects and above all geometrical ones, whereas disordered things are remembered poorly and with difficulty. For just as with objects of perception, if they lie in sequence and in order, sight sees well, but if confusedly, not well, so too with the impressions in the soul. Recollecting differs from learning again, and in general learning differs from recollection, in that the one who recollects is moved from himself and the starting point within him to what is continuous with that starting point, whereas the learner is moved not through himself but through another, the teacher. Further, often one who is recollecting is at first unable to recollect something at once, but by searching and taking great pains he is nevertheless able in the end and finds it. This happens to one who sets many [motions] going, until he sets going a motion of the kind on which the thing will follow. For just as the many drops made the rock fit [to be worn], and in the end the last one hollowed it, so it is with the moisture in the heart: having been moved many times, it is moved with a last motion, by which what is sought rises up. | Recollecting, then, is the presence within of the moving power, and by power I mean the existing starting point. For this sharpens the mind and rouses it to unravel the rest, and this in such a way that it is moved from itself and from the motions it holds within, as has been said. That is why one must take hold of a starting point. Hence people seem sometimes to recollect most quickly from places; and by places we mean either the starting points that we say must be present in the soul, or those based on coordinates, similars and opposites, as has been said in the Dialectic, or bodily places and positions in such and such a part. The cause is that one passes quickly from one thing to another, for example from milk to white, from white to air, from this to moist, from which one remembered autumn, when seeking this season. For the most part the middle seems to be a starting point for everything, and finding it helps greatly, for it guides one to the grasp of what is sought. For example, let these letters be set out, equal in number and corresponding to the thoughts of the soul with which it is moved when recollecting in order to find what is sought: ABΓΔEZHΘ. And since E is the middle, whoever has found it, if he does not find what he was seeking together with finding E, will remember it on coming to Θ. For once one has taken hold of the middle, it is possible to be moved both forward and backward. Nothing prevents one from making the thoughts out of order and in reverse, and thinking Θ after E, and from Θ Z, then H. If, then, what is sought is among the ones ahead, he will find it thus on coming to Θ, as has been said; if among the ones behind, on coming to A. | The thoughts corresponding to the letters are these: Athens, the Lyceum, Plato's house, the new-moon day, a drinking party, Socrates, being struck by Socrates, a lyre.

The reason why from the same [starting point] one sometimes remembers and sometimes does not is that several movements can be set going from the same starting point. For example, from the side (pleura) one might set out towards the thought both of pleurisy and of Pleurone. If, then, pleurisy is more familiar than Pleurone, it will draw the mind more towards itself, as bright bodies draw the sight. And not only for these reasons: if one of the impressions is old and the other new, the new one will move [the soul] more towards recollecting it, unless perhaps the old one has been stamped in deeply, as a scientific state, and is moreover familiar; for it is as good as new through daily practice. And just as some things follow one another by nature (for by nature heat follows the recollection of fire, and illumination that of the sun), so also by habit. For there are some things, from habit, on recollecting which we at once recollect also the things that come after them. What has often been made habitual is like nature, and since in things that happen by nature error also occurs, and what is contrary to nature, this can also happen in things that happen through habit. If so, nothing prevents one who has recollected the prior and leading item from going wrong about the later and following one, and being moved otherwise than he should, and especially when pleurisy drags [the mind] away from Pleurone. This is also why, when we need to recollect a name, | we remember another similar one and make a blunder in respect of that one. For someone who wishes to recollect Leophanes and remembers Leosthenes has blundered with regard to Leophanes.

Recollecting, then, happens in this way. To speak generally about memory and recollection: the most important thing in both is that one must recognise the time, either by measure and definitely (as: what I remember or recollect I saw yesterday, or a month ago), or indefinitely, as: I simply perceived it before, and saw and heard this long ago. For if this did not happen, we would suppose that we were not recollecting or remembering, but putting these things forward now for the first time and from ourselves. What judges the longer and shorter time in such cases is the primary perceptive soul, seated in the heart. For as the mind judges magnitudes not by reaching out towards them, in the way those who make seeing consist in an emission of rays say that we see, but by moving the impressions from the magnitudes that are stored up in the imagination (for if it judged in that way, it could not judge when they were not present; but as it is, it judges even when they are absent; for the mind is nothing other than the activity of intellect together with imagination), so it is reasonable to hold that the perceptive soul too judges the longer and shorter time while staying within and being moved by the impressions present in it. And since in the remembering of comprehensive and universal accounts the particular and included ones are also grasped together, and when we remember by heart a whole section from a book and a long | period, we also think of its parts (for the whole is made of parts, and the parts here are clauses and phrases), in what will recollection through all of them together and in common differ from recollection in part? Or [does it differ] in so far as here, with the memory of the whole, one happens also to think of the part, and there, with that of the universal, also of the particular? Yet one will think of the inner and smaller items before the extremes and the whole; and the inner items are proportional both to one another and to the extremes, by being joined to each other and coming in order, like those words in the Timaeus: "Gods of gods, of whom I am the craftsman and father of works, which, having come to be through me, are indissoluble unless I will it. Now everything that has been bound is dissoluble, but to wish to dissolve what has been well fitted together and is in a good state belongs to one who is bad. Therefore, since you have come to be, you are not immortal nor wholly indissoluble, yet you will not be dissolved nor meet the fate of death." When the whole is thought, the part is thought together with it; yet the mind went over "gods of gods" before what follows it, and that before the next, and the common [whole] last of all; for the particulars together are the whole. As it is with things and thoughts, so it is reasonable to inquire about time; for time is strung together with thoughts, as it were, and knowledge along with them. Hence also, as the smaller thing is to the larger, so the smaller time will be to the larger, and alternately, as the whole thing is to the whole time, so are the parts to the parts. This will be clearer in a diagram. | Let two triangles be set out with their vertices downward, one placed within the other, and let KMN be the containing one and ABE the contained one; and let AB be cut at the points Γ and Z, and let ΓΔ and ZH be joined to the opposite side of the same triangle, in straight lines; and let KM also be cut at Θ and Λ, and let ΘΞ and ΛP be joined to the opposite side of the same triangle, in straight lines; and let the sections of the lines of both triangles lie in a straight line. Let the smaller and inner [triangle] be the things the soul thinks, and the larger and outer the time perceived along with the thoughts. Just as, then, one who has been moved through AB, BE has at the same time been moved through AΓ, ΓΔ (for they are within and contained), so one who [has been moved through] AΓ, ΓΔ [has also been moved through] AZ, ZH. For as AΓ is to AB, so is ΓΔ to BE; for they are proportional, and hence also alternately. Again, as AZ is to AΓ, so is ZH to ΓΔ, and alternately. Finally, just as one who thinks the whole lines | AB and BE thinks together with them also AΓ, ΓΔ, which are parts, so one who [thinks] AΓ, ΓΔ [thinks also] AZ, ZH. And as it is with these, so with time. For one who has been moved through the temporal lines KM, MN has also been moved through KΘ, ΘΣ, and further through KΛ, ΛP. KM, MN was the time of the thing AB, BE (for it was gathered together with the thinking of that), KΘ, ΘΞ the time of AΓ, ΓΔ, and KΛ, ΛP that of AZ, ZH; for all are together and proportional. It is clear, then, that when remembering or recollecting we of necessity also think of the time that fills [it].

Deception in memory happens in two ways. One way is when an exchange occurs regarding the things remembered and the impressions, for example if the soul, seeing the image of Theaetetus, were to suppose it to be of Socrates; for then it will think it remembers Socrates while remembering Theaetetus; for nothing prevents someone from being mistaken and thinking he remembers when he does not remember. The second is when I remember something but am not aware of it because of some other movement, just as often, while reasoning something out and thinking, I do not see the person standing in front of me, so that I am then like someone dreaming and not aware that he is dreaming. There is, then, no memory or recollection unless the movement of the time follows upon the movement of the thing, and on top of these, awareness. The time, as has been said, we sometimes remember indefinitely, sometimes definitely. For sometimes one does not remember it by measure, for example that I did it two days ago or a month ago, but simply that I did this at some time long ago; and sometimes by measure too. A sign of remembering without measure is what people usually say, that they re|member, but do not know when, when they do not recognise it by a definite measure.

That those good at remembering and those good at recollecting are not the same has been said earlier. Remembering also differs from recollecting not only in time (for memory comes before recollection), but also because many of the other animals share in remembering, but in recollection, one may say, none of the known animals except man; for whoever has recollection also has reasoning. For as one who reasons joins this premise to that, so one who recollects [joins] the smaller to the greater. Whoever has reasoning also has inquiry, and this belongs to those who have deliberation. So whoever has recollection also has will; but man alone deliberates, so man alone also recollects. That recollecting belongs to the mind has been shown, for deliberating belongs to intellect. But since it is impossible to do this without imagination (for it recollects by moving the images in the heart and the breath in it), the affection is something bodily, and recollection is an impulse of the mind in such an image. For as one who wishes to read seeks the book and sees what is written in it, so here too the mind resembles the reader, the heart the book, and the images the letters. A sign that the affection of memory and recollection is bodily is that some people are disturbed against their will when, trying, they cannot recollect. And indeed, though they hold back their mind completely and do not allow it to search further, they nonetheless go on searching, since, once the heart or the moisture in it has been moved in our attempt to recollect, it is no longer readily willing to stop, and we experience something like someone dragging us against our | will to turn towards him. Melancholics are especially troubled by such images; for being easily moved, as being filled with much thick breath in the heart, whenever a movement of one image occurs, at once a great many are stirred up in heaps through the easy mobility of the moisture of the heart. And since often, wishing to recollect, we cannot, either not at all or not when we wish, the reason is that it is not in our power; but just as those who throw a stone cannot stop its flight, so the one who recollects, like one hunting, moves something bodily in which the affection lies (for nothing incorporeal is moved of itself); this is why it is not in his power to stop it. And just as for one who has set out to read this passage merely opening the book is not enough unless he also finds the place, so it is with the mind and the images in the heart; for it will not remember by moving the images unless it lights upon what it seeks. Hence, as has been said, those are most troubled in whom there happens to be moisture around the perceptive place; for once moved they do not easily stop until they come upon what is sought and the movement runs straight. This is also why angers and fears, when they have moved something, do not settle down when those things move in return, but move back again towards the same thing for a time. For example, the heart, moved in angers and rages after reason has judged, by the boiling blood, and heated more because it is firmer, heats the blood in return. And in fears too, when the opposites occur, cooling and contraction, [people] are not easily restored; and the affection is like | names, tunes and words; for when one of them has been much on someone's lips, it comes back to them to sing or say again even when they have stopped and do not wish to. Those who have their upper parts larger, and dwarfish people, are also more forgetful than their opposites, because they have much weight upon the perceptive faculty and can neither retain the movements from the start, but they are dissolved, nor run straight easily in recollecting; and the very young and the very old are forgetful because of movement; for the former are in growth, the latter in much decay. Further, children are dwarfish up to a late age. About memory and remembering, then, what their nature is and by which part of the soul animals remember, and about recollecting, what it is, how it comes about, and through what cause, has been said.
ON SLEEP AND WAKING.

1. About sleep and waking we must consider what they are and in what part of the soul [they occur], and whether they are proper to the soul or also to the body, and through what cause they belong to animals, and whether all [animals] share in both, or some only in sleep and others only in the other; and besides these, what the dream is, and through what cause sleepers sometimes dream and sometimes do not dream, and whether it happens that sleepers always dream but do not remember, or not, and if it does happen, through what cause it comes about; and whether it is possible to foresee the future or [not] possible, and in what way, if it is possible; and whether [only] things that are going to be done by a human being, or also those of which the divine holds the cause, and [which] come about by nature or by chance. And first this at least is clear, that waking and sleep belong to the same part of the animal; for they are opposed, and sleep appears to be a kind of privation of waking. And extremes and opposites always appear, both in things of art and in things of nature, to come about in the same receptive subject, and are affections of the same thing; I mean, for example, harmony | and disharmony [are] about the same thing, and order and disorder, and further disease and health [are] about the same thing, for [they are] in a body; ugliness and beauty in the organic [parts], strength and weakness in the sinews, and again about sight [there are] sight and blindness, and similarly in hearing. Further, it is clear also from the following: for that by which we recognise someone awake, by this we also [recognise] someone asleep. We recognise someone awake by his perceiving either some movement of things outside, as seeing or hearing, or of things inside and within himself, as reasoning and imagining; and again we call asleep the one who is active with no movement either of external things or of internal ones. Perception and absence of perception [are] as possession and privation, and these will belong to one and the same thing; so sleep and waking too will have the same subject.

Since perceiving is proper neither to the soul nor to the body (for that which has the capacity also has the activity, and what is called perception in activity is a kind of movement of the soul through the body), it is clear that the affection is neither proper to the soul, nor can a soulless body perceive, but [it belongs] to the compound of both. Since it has been determined earlier about what are called parts [of the soul], and the nutritive is separated from the others, while none of the others exists without it, it is clear that those living things that share only in growth and decay, such as plants, have neither sleep nor waking; for they do not have the perceptive part, in which these [are]. That the perceptive is different from the nutritive in being and in capacity is clear; whether also in subject is not clear to everyone. Further, of mortal things beneath the moon that are receptive of sleep and waking | there is none that is always awake or always asleep; but both these affections belong to the same animals, and there is no animal deprived of both; for this belongs to soulless things. Let the divine beings, however, which are always active, be excepted even among these; for the waking in them has no opposite. Sleep and waking, as has often been said, are affections concerning the perception of the primary perceptive faculty, the heart. Further, for all things that have some natural work, whenever [a thing] exceeds the time during which it is naturally fitted to do this, it must grow weary and, being unable to go on, stop. For beasts of burden carry a load up to a point, but if someone forces them further, they fall; and someone will read up to a point, then will grow weary; and a sculptor and a carpenter and anyone whatever will be active up to a point, then rest will succeed the movement. In the same way also eyes and ears, and further hands and feet and every organ. If, then, perceiving is the work of something, [doing it] continuously it will become incapable and will no longer do it; for the parts, having measured out the time that fills [their] capacity, will stop. If, then, sleeping is the opposite of being awake, and of opposites without intermediate, or of those according to possession and privation, if one is not present to the receptive subject the other must be present, then when waking is not present sleep will be present; and if excess of waking is sometimes diseased (for some have continued even up to nine days sleepless through illness), and sometimes without disease, as those who have suffered this very thing through emaciation or drying, then incapacity, and long sleep too, will come about sometimes | through disease and sometimes without disease; for someone who had a fever continued sleeping for three days, and infants and those who are moister in diet or temperament sleep for a very great length of time. If this is so, then everything that is awake sleeps and what sleeps wakes. For if sleep is an affection of the perceptive part and as it were a kind of binding and immobility, and the perceptive is what is able to perceive in activity, and every capacity is brought into activity, then what sleeps and has the capacity to wake must become awake, and no sleep is unwakable. Nearly all other [animals] are clearly seen to share in sleep, both swimming and flying and walking; for all the kinds of fishes and of cephalopods have been seen sleeping, and all the others that have eyes; for hard-eyed [animals] and insects are evidently seen sleeping too, but all such are short sleepers; hence it might often escape someone whether they share in sleeping or not. Of the testaceans, it has not yet become clear to perception whether they sleep; but if the argument stated is persuasive to anyone, he will be persuaded of this. That all animals share in sleep, then, is clear from these things; for the animal is defined by having perception, and sleep we call in a way the immobility and as it were binding of perception, and the release and the rousing [we call] waking. None of the plants can share in either of the affections; for without perception there is neither sleep nor waking; and those that have perception also have being pained and rejoicing, and those that have these [have] also desire. But none of these belongs to plants. No argument will compel [us to say] that plants are pleased or pained or in general de|sire or perceive; nor does the perceptive follow on every nutritive [part], as the reverse [does], but it is separated. A sign is that the nutritive part also does its own work more in sleeping than in being awake; for [animals] are nourished and grow more then, as needing perception not at all for these things.

Why [an animal] sleeps and wakes, and through what perception, or what [perceptions], if [it is] more than one, must be considered. Since some animals have all the senses, and some do not have [some], for example sight, but all have touch and taste, and touch is the most common of all, as has been said in the [books] On the Soul, and it is impossible for the sleeping animal to perceive with any sense whatever without qualification, it is clear that the same affection must belong to all [the senses] in what is called [sleep], I mean complete immobility and absence of perception. For if [the animal] were active in one of the senses, say hearing, but not in another, for example sight, opposites will occur at the same time in the same thing; for while asleep it will perceive. But this is impossible. Must we, then, blame all [the senses] equally for the said affections, or some more and some not? Or just one only (and this is touch), as more necessary and prior by nature to the others and identical in subject with the common sense? For since there belongs to each sense something proper and something common, proper as, for example, seeing to sight, hearing to hearing, and to each of the others in the same way, and there is also a common capacity accompanying these, by which [the animal perceives] that it sees and hears and per|ceives (for it does not, of course, see by sight that it sees), and judges and is able to judge that sweet things are different from white ones, neither by taste nor by sight nor by both, but by a certain common part of all the perceptive faculties, which we also call without qualification and properly the common sense, whose sense organ is also most common and properly one, and [it is] one, but in account more than one and as many as the subjects of the particular [senses]; for colour is different from sound, and smell from both; and this [common sense] belongs at once and primarily and most of all to the tactile [faculty]; for this is separated from the other sense organs, but the others are inseparable from it. These things have been discussed in the studies On the Soul), it is clear that waking and sleep belong to this, namely to the common sense, in the common sense organ, the heart. We joined this sense with touch in subject, and therefore it belongs to all animals; for touch alone [belongs] to all. That sleep is an idleness of touch alone and first, and not simply of the senses in common, may be clear from this: for if it is not necessary for all to be active at once, neither will all be immobile at once. But the first [is true] (for what necessity is there that one who sees should at once also hear, or one who tastes see?), so the second too. For the opposite would have been more reasonable to happen to them, that all are active at once, rather than immobile at once. But if being active at once is not possible, which is more reasonable, much more neither [is] being immobile [at once]. Yet when touch is idle, all [the others are idle] too. Still, sleep does not come from the idleness of all, but from that of the first one alone, the tactile. For when the [organ] in control of the other sense organs and to which the others ex|tend is affected in some way, all the rest must be affected along with it, but when one of those is incapable, it is not necessary that this be incapable.

Further, it is still more clearly evident from the following that sleep does not consist in the senses being idle and not using them, nor in being unable to perceive. For in fainting fits something of this sort happens; for fainting is an incapacity of all the senses, but it is not sleep. Certain derangements of this kind also occur; for madmen neither see nor hear nor perceive with any other sense. For how [could they], when they devour their own flesh and receive no perception of any pain? And if someone ties the two veins in the neck, the animal becomes insensible, but this is not sleep. Rather, when the incapacity of perceiving arises neither in some one of the sense organs (for it might happen that someone's sense organs are maimed and unable to perceive, and this is not sleeping) nor through any chance cause, but, as has just been said, in the primary sense organ, the heart, and in the primary sense, and through excess of being awake, this is sleep. For when this is incapable, all the sense organs must also be incapable of perceiving; but when one of those [is], it is not necessary for this [one to be].

These things having been thus determined, we must now state both for what cause sleeping comes about and what sort of affection it is. Since there are several modes of cause (for in the works on nature we have set out four as the more authoritative: there we called that for the sake of which the final cause, and the efficient that from which the starting point of motion [comes], and the formal the account according to which the thing comes | to be, and in addition to all these the matter, from which, as present within it, something is brought to completion), the cause of sleep, as that for the sake of which, would be the preservation and rest of animals; the efficient [cause] the motion of the cardiac *pneuma* [breath, vital spirit]; the material the ebbing back downwards of the exhalation that has been carried up; and the formal such a collapse and disposition of the outer and inner limbs and parts. For it is as follows. First, since we say that nature acts for the sake of something, and this is some good, and that rest is necessary and beneficial to what is naturally disposed to move but cannot move always and continuously with pleasure, it is clear that sleep is for the sake of the preservation of animals; hence, on account of the very truth of the matter, people apply this metaphor to sleep, calling it alone of all things rest. Waking is the end; for perceiving and thinking are the end for all to which either of them belongs; for these are best, and the end is best; and the end for irrational [animals] is perception, for humans understanding. Further, sleep must belong to each of the animals on account of matter of this kind, which we are accustomed to call necessity on hypothesis. For if there is to be an animal having its own nature, certain things must of necessity belong to it, and when these belong, other things [must] belong. For example, when it is supposed that there is an animal, being nourished follows of necessity, and when it is nourished, exhalation comes about, and when this is completed, sleep. Further, what sort of motion and activity arising in the body brings about waking and sleeping in animals, and in general the efficient cause, must be discussed after this. The account of it will be rather long. But first we say this: that for some, such as the bloodless, one must suppose that the | causes of the affection are either the same or analogous, and for the blooded the same as for humans, so that one must study all cases starting from these as closer [to us]. That the starting point of perception in animals arises from the same part as that of motion has been determined earlier in other works. This is, of three determined places, the middle one between the head and the lower belly. In the blooded, then, this is the region around the heart; for all blooded [animals] have a heart, and so the starting point of motion and of the controlling perception is from there. As to motion, it is evident that the starting point of breath and in general of cooling is there, and nature has made breathing and cooling by liquid for the preservation of the heat in this part. It will be discussed later by itself. In the bloodless, both insects and those that do not take in breath, the innate *pneuma* is seen swelling up and subsiding in the analogous [part]. This is clear in the whole-winged, such as wasps and bees, and in flies and the like. For in these we clearly see the part near the segmentation widening and contracting. Since it is impossible to move or do anything without strength, and the holding and retention of breath produces strength, for those that take it in and breathe it will be [breath] from outside, for those that do not breathe the innate [breath]. That is why winged [insects] are seen to buzz when they move; for the innate *pneuma*, being rubbed in flight and striking against the diaphragm of the whole-winged, buzzes. For it is not the outside air that makes the sound, | but the innate *pneuma*. Buzzing also comes about through the outside [air] in those insects that have a slit beneath the diaphragm. Everything moves when some perception, either its own or foreign, arises in the primary sense organ: we call it its own on account of the impulse from within (for we are moved also by certain images within us), and foreign on account of [the impulse] from without, that is, from the objects of perception. It is evident, then, from these things in what place and in what part first sleep and waking arise. For [they arise] in that whose affections they are, and they are affections of the heart, so [they arise] in it. Some people move while asleep and do many waking acts, yet not without some image and perception; for the dream is in a way a perception. But these must be discussed later. Why people remember dreams when they have woken but do not remember waking actions has been stated by us in the *Problems*.

These things then having been determined beforehand, what comes next to what has been said is to state upon what occurrences and from where the starting point of the affection, of waking and sleeping, arises; for perhaps in these we would better find the efficient cause, and the material more completely. It is evident, then, that it is necessary for the animal, when it has perception, then first to be an animal and to take nourishment and growth. For it is nourished even while it is an embryo, but not as an animal, rather as a plant; when it acquires perception, then first it is nourished as an animal. The perceptive [soul] comes to be in it later, after it is born. The final nourishment for all is, for the blooded, the nature of blood, and for the bloodless its analogue. The places of blood are the veins, | and their starting point is the heart. What has been said is evident from dissections. When the nourishment from outside enters the receptive places, I mean the stomach and intestines, the exhalation into the veins comes about; carried off by them into the liver, it is changed there and turned into blood, and travelling thence to the starting point, the heart, it is properly concocted and becomes perfect blood. For of the veins some run to the heart and others begin from there. For some, like servants, carry to it from the places around the liver the unworked and unconcocted blood, which it receives, concocts and works up; the others fulfil the opposite service, the conveying [of it] after concoction and working up to the whole body. These things have been discussed more fully in the works on nourishment; now they must be taken up again for this purpose, that we may study the starting points of the motion, and through what affection of the perceptive part waking and sleep come about. For sleep is not any incapacity whatever of the perceptive [part], as has been said; for derangement, a certain choking, and fainting also produce such incapacity, and some people who have fainted severely have already had imagination too, and see [things]. This, then, contains a certain difficulty too: for if it is possible for one who has fainted to fall asleep, it would be possible for his image to be a dream as well. But the first is not [so], so neither is the second. For it is clear that, if not all, yet most dreams we remember when woken, but [people] remember none of the images in fainting fits after recovery. There are many things which those who have fainted severely and seemed to have died say at the time, | none of which they remember when roused. So their images are not dreams, so that the seizure is not sleep either. The same must be said also about choking and derangement and the like.

But, as we said, sleep is not every incapacity of the perceptive [part]; rather, this affection arises from the exhalation connected with nourishment. For what is exhaled, being pushed, must be pushed up to a certain point, and then turn back and change [direction] like a euripus. For the heat of each animal naturally rises upward, but when it reaches the upper places and is made colder than itself by the temperament of the brain, it turns back again all at once and is carried down to the heart and cools the heat in it, and so the animal sleeps. That is why sleep comes chiefly after nourishment: for much of the moist and the bodily is carried [up] all at once. So while it remains in the head, it weighs it down (which is also why we move it this way and that when nodding off), but when the heat that brought the moist bodily [matter] up turns back and sinks, these also flow down together with it, and so sleep comes about, and then the animal sleeps. A sign that the moist and bodily [matter] weighs down the head comes also from soporifics: for all of them, both drinks and foods, poppy, mandrake, wine, darnel, plainly produce heaviness of the head through the thickness of the upward flow of the bodily moisture from them. So such sleep comes chiefly after food (for the exhalation from food is great), but it also comes from certain kinds of fatigue; for fatigue is colliquative, and the | colliquation becomes like undigested nourishment, unless it is cold. For the heat from the fatigue, having melted the residues present in the stomach and the intestines, sent them to the upper place and produced sleep. Certain diseases also do this very thing, those that come from moist and hot residue, as happens to those with fever and in lethargies. Further, in the first age sleep is greater than in the others; for small children sleep a great deal because all the nourishment is carried upward. A sign of this is that in the first age the size of the upper parts exceeds that of the lower, because growth takes place in them. For the parts in which the nourishment is greater are larger. For this reason they are also subject to epilepsy; for sleep is like a seizure, since each is an idleness of the senses. That is why for some people the onset of this affection occurs while they are asleep, and they are seized while asleep, whenever they are bound to suffer it, but not while awake. For the *pneuma*, as has been said, being carried upward in great quantity in sleep, coming down again like a euripus swells the veins. For as this goes down and another goes up, because the evaporation takes place below at the same time as the cooling and condensation above, the veins must swell, and by them the passage of respiration is pressed together and contracted; when it is narrowed, inhalation necessarily fails, and from this comes the seizure. Since in small children the upper parts are full of nourishment, which is the same as saying of *pneuma* from the nourishment distributed, and since wine is pneumatic too, and dark wine more than other kinds, it is not good for them, nor for their wet-nurses; for it perhaps makes no difference whether they drink it themselves or their nurses do, but they ought to drink it watered and little. The upper parts of small children are so full | of nourishment that at five months they cannot even turn their neck. The affection is similar in those who are very drunk; for in both cases much moisture has been carried upward. It is reasonable to say that this affection is also the cause of embryos being at rest in the womb at first.

And in general those whose veins are not visible, the dwarfish and the large-headed are given to sleep. For in the first the veins are narrow and thin, so that the *pneuma*, coming down from the head, easily fills them; for what is small is filled more quickly. For this reason, when the veins become cold (for the passages [need] heat in order to flow through and disperse), and the *pneuma* lingers, sleep is necessarily also longer. Besides, just as water passes slowly through narrow pipes but more quickly through wide ones, so too the bodily *pneuma* will pass more slowly through the passages. Those whose veins are not visible are given to sleep for this reason. In the dwarfish and large-headed the upward impulse and exhalation are great; for large things need much nourishment in order to be filled and sated. So when much goes up, it follows that the backflow downward is also great, and much [matter], from perhaps the same heat, is slowly digested and mastered. Those with prominent veins are not sleepy, because of the free flow of the passages, unless they have some other contrary affection; nor are melancholics. For their inner region is chilled, so that no quantity of exhalation arises in them. For this reason they are voracious, being dry. For their bodies are in a state as if they had not benefited [from food], like wood lying in a dry place. For black bile, being cold by nature, | makes cold both the nutritive parts, stomach and liver, and the other parts, wherever the power of such residue is present. And since we often nod off while reading and thinking, it should be understood that the cause is that the mind is then in motion and concentration; for since the nourishment is undigested on this account, the vapour going up and coming down must be thick. So it is evident from what has been said that sleep is a certain concentration of the heat inward to the heart and a natural counter-displacement for the stated cause. Where the heat fails, [the part] is chilled, and through chilling the eyelids droop; for it is the heat that holds together, moves and keeps upright all the parts. So in sleep the upper and outer parts and those around the whole body are chilled, while the inner and lower parts are warm, such as those around the feet and the internal parts.

Yet someone might raise this difficulty: why sleep is stronger after food, and wine and other things having such heat are soporific. For it is not reasonable that sleep should be a chilling while the causes of sleeping are hot. Or does this happen, first, because, just as the stomach is hot when empty but its filling chills it (for the filling with food stifles and extinguishes the heat, as a quantity of wood does fire), so too the veins and the passages in the head are chilled by the quantity of the exhalation carried up, and when this happens the exhalation condenses and flows downward, and for this reason sleep comes after food? And second, just as shivering comes upon those over whom hot [water] is suddenly poured (for when the hot is poured over, the cold outside, being displaced, concentrated into one and gathered by its flight inward, causes shivering), so in that | case too, as the heat rises to the head, the cold distributed from the brain into those places is gathered and, becoming one and very strong through its concentration into one, chills [it] and makes the moist and hot [matter] naturally carried up there lose its strength, condense and withdraw downward. And besides these, just as fire is extinguished when logs are piled on, so when much nourishment comes in the heat in the heart is chilled and, as it were, extinguished, until the nourishment is digested. For sleep comes about, as has been said, in the turning back toward the starting point of the bodily moisture carried up by the heat through the veins to the head. For when what has been carried up can no longer stay above, but exceeds by its quantity and weighs [it] down and is moreover chilled, it is pushed back again and flows downward. That is why people also drop when nodding off, as the heat that carries [them] up and holds [them] upright is drawn away and flows downward. Man, then, sleeps lying down because he alone of animals is upright, and [the heat] falling back produces first derangement and complete insensibility, and later imagination. Or rather, the solutions stated are possible and are given with a view to the plausible rather than the true, but that [following] one will be the proper one, and this is more truly the cause of sleeping. For the region around the brain, as has been said elsewhere, is the coldest of all in the body, and in those which do not have [a brain], the part analogous to it. And just as the moisture evaporating from the earth and the waters through the heat of the sun, when it comes into the upper | region, is chilled through its coldness, condenses, and is carried down, becoming water again, so in the upward movement of the heat to the brain the residual exhalation condenses into phlegm (which is why catarrhs evidently come from the head), while the nutritive and not unhealthy [exhalation] is carried down and, condensing, chills the heat. The narrowness and thinness of the veins around the brain also contribute to its being chilled and not easily receiving the exhalation. For because of their thinness they have little heat, and what is little is more easily affected.

This, then, is the cause of the chilling and of sleep. One wakes when the heat, much of it crowded together into a small space from the surrounding parts, has completed digestion and prevailed, and when the more corporeal blood and the purest have been separated. The thinnest and purest blood is that in the head, the thickest and most turbid that in the lower parts. The starting point of all the blood, as has been said both here and elsewhere, is the heart; and of the [chambers] in the heart the middle one is common to each of the two chambers, and each of those receives [blood] from one of the two veins, the one called the great [vein] and the aorta, which bring the blood from the liver still undigested and unworked, and in the middle one the separation takes place. But to determine these matters belongs more properly to other treatises. Because the blood becomes less separated after the taking of food, sleep comes on, until the purer part of the blood has been separated upward and the more turbid downward; and when this happens, [animals] wake, released from the weight of the | food.

So it has been said what the cause of sleeping is: that it is the counter-displacement, all at once, by the corporeal matter carried up by the innate heat, onto the primary sense organ; and what sleep is: that it is a seizing of the primary sense organ so that it cannot be active, which occurs by necessity (for the animal cannot exist unless the things that produce and preserve it occur, among which was nourishment, from which comes the exhalation), but for the sake of preservation; for rest preserves.
ON DREAMS.

1. After this we must inquire about dreams, and first to which [part] of the soul they appear, and whether this affection belongs to the intellective or to the perceptive [part]; for these are the only things in us by which we come to know anything. That it belongs simply to neither is clear. For if the use of sight is seeing, and of hearing hearing, and in general of perception perceiving, and the capacities exist for the sake of the activities; and if of the perceptibles in the senses some are common and others proper, common such as magnitude and motion (for they fall under several [senses]) and the other such things, and proper such as colour, sound, flavour, the first for sight, the second for hearing, the third for taste; and if all animals are unable to see when their eyes are closed and they are asleep, and likewise in the case of the remaining [senses], so that we perceive nothing in sleep: then it is not by perception that we perceive the dream. But neither are dreams affections of the mind or of opinion. For since in sleep we not only assent that what approaches is a horse or a man or in general a substance, but also that it is white <or> beautiful, and opinion does not | grasp these without perception, and perception is not active in sleep, then dreams do not belong to opinion or to thinking either.

Further, besides the dream we often think of something else. For just as in waking, when we perceive something, we often think something further about it, so too in sleep we sometimes think of other things besides the images. For someone who sees Socrates in sleep thinks that he is seeing him in sleep; just as I too, seeing that I had found a book which I had long wanted, thought that I was seeing this in a dream; and my companion, seeing our most revered master [as if] he had risen from the dead, thought while still asleep that he was seeing his teacher risen in a dream. And someone too who saw in sleep that he had found gold, while still held by sleep seemed to be telling his friends that he had found a treasure in his sleep. But [this happens] not always, whereas with opinion we are always aware, of what we opine, that we opine it. So in this way too dreams do not belong to opinion. At the same time it is clear that not every image in sleep is a dream; but when someone sees something and does not think that what he sees is a dream, that is a dream; whereas when, while seeing, he can think that what is seen is a dream, this is then an image, but in no way a dream. For things seem to be dreams which are not, but images; and these come from the perceptions in activity that occur at the onset of sleep, when we have been able to grasp that they were imagined while we were awake. For in a certain way it is waking to be able to think that what is seen is a dream. That we often think of something else is clear to those who try to remember their dreams after getting up. For just as some who try to remember sayings learned by heart remember them better than those who learn them by heart without | trying to remember, because the former, following the dialectical precept, place what is put to them in a mnemonic place, and the latter do not, so too with dreams those who have trained themselves to remember their dreams remember better, after getting up, what they saw. This happens when someone, as soon as he gets up from sleep, immediately goes over again what he had seen in sleep.

From all this at least this much is clear: that the same thing by which we are deceived when awake in illnesses also produces the deception in sleep. For just as in illnesses the thick pneuma rising up, because of its thickness and the violent motion from the fever, throws the visual pneuma into confusion and makes us be deceived and think that one thing is two, and that the lines on the walls are animals (for the forms of the lines, falling without matter on the sight, and being thrown together somehow and combined because of the motion of the visual pneuma, produce the appearance of an animal), so too in sleep such pneuma becomes the cause of deception for us. Even those who are healthy and know [better] are not prevented from being deceived, either because of the size of the distance or because the sight is affected in some way; for the sun seems a foot across, and the land seems to move to those on a ship. If this is so, much more [are] the sick [deceived], and still more [people] in sleep. But whether the imaginative [part] of the soul and the perceptive are the same or different, there is no deception at all without seeing or in general perceiving something; for to see or hear wrongly belongs to one who sees and hears something real, but not what he thinks. But in sleep it is assumed that one sees nothing, hears nothing, and in general perceives nothing. Is it then true that one sees nothing, but not true that one perceives nothing, and is it possible that sight is affected in some way, and | the other senses? For [the sense organs] carry the residues from the perceptibles even in sleep, each of which, just as when we are awake, strikes the perceptive starting point, the heart; and sometimes the mind says that it is false and has become aware that it is a dream, when the descending exhalation is not much and we are as if awake; but sometimes it is held fast, when what descends is a great quantity, and it follows the image as true, viewing the impressions of things as the things themselves. That the affection we call dreaming does not belong to the opining faculty, nor to the reasoning or in general the thinking faculty, is evident; but neither does it belong simply to the perceiving faculty; for then one would necessarily see and hear simply. But how, and in what way, must be examined.

Let it be laid down, as is evident, that the affection belongs to the perceptive [part], since sleep does too; for sleep does not belong to one part of animals and dreaming to another, but to the same.
