And since imagination has been discussed in On the Soul, and the imaginative is the same as the perceptive, though being imaginative and being perceptive are different, and imagination is the motion arising from perception in activity even when the perceptibles are not present, and the dream appears to be a kind of image (for we call the image in sleep a dream, whether it arises simply or in a certain way), it is evident that dreaming belongs to the perceptive [part], but to it as imaginative.

What the dream is and how it comes about we may best see from what happens in connection with sleep. For the perceptibles produce perception in us in each sense | organ, and the affections and residues produced by them are present in the sense organs not only while the senses are active but also after they have gone; and of these, those that are preserved and not wholly obliterated by the quantity of exhalation, striking the perceptive starting point in sleep because of the ebbing of the pneuma downward at that time, and moving perception in a manner closely similar to perception in activity, produce dreams. So when the exhalation is great, so that it escapes our notice and we cannot grasp that we are awake, we are deceived, and seeing the semblances and residues of the perceptibles we think we see and hear those very true perceptibles; but when the blood-exhalation is not so great but moderate, so that it does not escape our notice, we are not deceived, but say while sleeping that this semblance appears to be Socrates, yet it is not, but the impression and residue of Socrates. It is clear, then, that the descending pneuma is the cause both of being deceived and of not being deceived, the same one that in illnesses is up above.

That the residue remains for some time in the sense organs even when the perceptibles are not present is clear from the following as well. For the affection seems to be closely similar in these cases and in the case of things that are carried along. For in the case of things carried along too, they are moved when what moved them is no longer touching them: the mover moved some air, and that air in turn, being moved, moved other air, and in this way, until it comes to rest, it produces the motion both in air and in liquids. One must suppose the same in the case of alteration as well. For | what has been heated by the hot heats what is near it, and this passes [the heat] on as far as the starting point. So in that in which perceiving takes place too, since perception in activity is a kind of alteration, this must happen. Therefore the affection is present not only in the sense organs while we perceive, but also when we have stopped, in the imaginative [part], both in depth and on the surface. This is evident when we perceive something continuously. For when we shift perception the affection follows along, as [when we pass] from the sun into an unlit and sunless place: it happens that we see nothing, because of the motion produced by the light that is still present in the eyes. And if we look at one colour for a long time, whether white or green, whatever we turn our sight to appears of that colour. And if, after looking at the sun or at something else bright, we close our eyes, then, if we watch, in the straight line in which sight happens to see, with the eyelids closed opposite the bright object, there appears first something of that colour; then it changes to crimson and then to purple, until it reaches the black colour and vanishes. The eyes are also changed by moving things, for instance by rivers, and especially by the fastest-flowing; for things at rest appear to be moving. And people also become poor at smelling similar [smells] after strong smells. These things plainly happen as we say.

That the sense organs perceive quickly even a small difference is shown by what happens with mirrors, a matter that one might examine and be puzzled about, if one attended to it on its own. At the same time it is clear from these that, just as sight is affected, so it also | acts in some way. For in very clean mirrors, when women look into the mirror while their menses are occurring, there forms on the surface of the mirror something like a bloody cloud. And if the mirror is new, it is not easy to wipe off such a stain, but if it is old, it is easier. The cause is, as we said, that sight is not only affected by the air but also acts and moves somewhat, as bright things also do; for the eye is among the things that have a bright colour. The eyes, then, at the time of such an affection are disposed like any other part of the whole body, reasonably enough; for all [the parts] are changed by the course of the menses, and they [the eyes] even more, being veiny. Therefore when the menses occur, through disturbance and bloody inflammation, in males the difference in their bodies is not evident (for when we gaze into a mirror during the emission of seed we do not move it along with us), but it is present (for seed and menses have the same nature); but because [seed] is white and similar to the mirror, it does not change it while moving along with it. The air, however, is moved by the menses, and makes the air over the mirror, which is continuous with it, of a certain quality and such as it is itself affected, and that air [affects] the surface of the mirror. And just as among garments the cleanest are stained most quickly (for what is clean shows precisely whatever it receives, and especially the smallest motions), so it is with these. Bronze, because it is smooth, makes the stains on it perceptible to us, and because it is clean, conspicuous. One must think of the contact of the air as a kind of rubbing, and as | wiping and washing. At any rate, just as sound arises most in smooth bodies, because in them the air is not broken nor chopped up at all into small pieces, so also in smooth mirrors the stains become conspicuous, because [the stain] remains one, as it were, owing to the smoothness of the mirror. The cause of its not going away more quickly from new mirrors is that they are clean and smooth; for it sinks through such [surfaces] both into depth and in every direction, into depth because of the cleanness, in every direction because of the smoothness. In old ones it does not remain, because the stain does not sink in in the same way, but more superficially. That motion arises even from small differences, that perception is quick, and further that the organ of colours is not only affected but also acts in return, is evident from these things. What happens with wines and with perfume-making also bears witness to what has been said. For prepared oil quickly takes on the smells of things nearby, and wines undergo this same thing; for they take on the smells not only of what is put into them or mixed in, but also of things placed near the vessels or growing [near them].

For the inquiry we began with, let one thing be laid down which is evident from what has been said: that even when the external perceptible has gone away, the sensations remain, being perceptible; and in addition, that we are easily deceived about our perceptions when we are in states of emotion, different people in different states, for instance the coward in fear, the lover in love, so that from a slight resemblance the one thinks he sees the enemy, the other his beloved; and the more emotional he is, the slighter | the resemblance from which this happens. In the same way, in fits of anger and in all desires, everyone becomes easily deceived, and the more so the more they are in these emotional states. That is why to people with fever animals sometimes appear on the walls, from a slight resemblance of lines put together; and this sometimes keeps pace with their condition in such a way that, if they are not very ill, it does not escape them that it is false, but if the affection is greater, they even move towards them. The cause of these things happening is that the authoritative [faculty], which is the mind, and that in which the images arise, which we presumably call perception, do not judge by the same power. A sign of this is that the sun appears to perception a foot across, but the intellect within contradicts it, [saying] that it is not as large as it appears. If they judged by the same power, it would be believed to be as large as it is seen to be. In some illnesses, however, nothing prevents the intellect too, when perception has been deranged, from falling ill along with it and holding the same opinion about the appearances, as some of the deranged think the lines and animals are moving. And why need one look for the difference in judgement between intellect and perception, when even among the senses themselves the account is not one, but the more authoritative have the more precise powers, as with touch and sight? For when the fingers are crossed, the one thing appears two to touch, but not to sight; for sight is more authoritative than touch. If touch were alone, or both had one judgement, we would judge the one thing to be two. The cause of being deceived is that anything whatever appears not only when the perceptible is moved, but also when perception itself is moved, if it is moved | in the same way as by the perceptible. I mean, for instance, the land seems [to move] to those sailing, when their sight is moved by something else.

From these things, then, it is evident that the motions arising from perceptions, both of external things and of those present from the body, occur not only when we are awake, but also when this affection called sleep comes about, and they appear even more at that time. For by day they are knocked out while the senses and the mind are active, and they vanish, just as a lesser fire beside a great one, and pains and pleasures beside great ones; but when these have stopped, even small things come to the surface. By night, however, because of the idleness of the particular senses and their inability to act, since the ebbing of the heat comes about from the outer parts to the inner, they are carried down to the starting point of perception, the heart, and become evident as the disturbance settles. One must suppose in these cases what [happens] with currents. For just as there it happens that the small eddies carried along in rivers are often alike, but often break up into other shapes because of the collision, so here too each motion comes about; by motion I mean the bringing of the residue to the heart as a semblance, by which the perceptive soul in it is roused. Just as there the change from one shape to another is not immediate, so too the motion of each semblance, which is in a substrate, the pneuma or the blood or the heart, when | it does not itself remain but is collided with, reaches the last [shape] through many intermediate ones. So the primary perception must be moved not only by that from which and that into which [the change occurs], but also by the intermediates. For just as, if this cloud resembles a lion, and then, changing through certain intermediates, comes to the likeness of a man, the soul has seen not only the shape of the lion and of the man but also the intermediates, whether they were pleasant and agreeable to it or otherwise painful and not cheering, so too the primary perception in sleep perceives not only the extremes but also the intermediates. And these are either altogether monstrous or gentle and natural. That is why dreams do not occur after food, nor to those who are very young, such as little children; for the motion is great because of the heat from the food. So, just as in a liquid, if one stirs it violently, sometimes no reflection appears, and sometimes one appears but entirely distorted, so that it appears different from what it was, but when it has come to rest [the reflections are] clear and plain, so too in sleep the images and the remaining motions that arise from the perceptions sometimes vanish entirely, when the said motion is greater, and sometimes the visions appear disturbed and monstrous and the dreams are worse, as for melancholics, those with fever and the drunk; for all such [states], being full of pneuma, produce much motion and disturbance. But when the blood settles and separates out in blooded animals, the motion of the sensations, preserved from each | of the senses, makes the dreams vigorous, and makes [things] both appear and seem [real]. For [one] seems to see what is carried down from sight, and to hear what comes from hearing, and similarly with what comes from the other sense organs; for because the motion arrives at the starting point from there, one seems, as though awake, to see and hear and in general to perceive. For if sight is not deceived in the crossing of the fingers in the way that touch is, neither will the perceptive soul be deceived in sleep; rather, the tactile power says the one thing is two, but the visual power holds out strongly against it and contradicts it, [saying] that what seem two are not two, but one. And if sight is not deceived in these matters, being more rational than touch, much more so is the criterion in the proper sense, the mind, provided it is not held fast by the excessive descent of the pneuma-laden fluid. For in general the starting point assents to what arrives at the starting point from each sense, unless another, more authoritative [faculty] contradicts it; for, simply, whatever touch or sight or any other of the senses conveys, the primary perception says it is such; so that if the one thing is reported as two by touch, or the sun as a foot across by vision, when there is nothing to judge further, the one thing appears as two, though not everything that appears is altogether believed, unless the judging [faculty] is held fast, as has often been said, or is not moved with its own and natural motion. And just as we said that different people are easily deceived through different affections, so the sleeper [is deceived] through | sleep and through the motion of the sense organs and the other things that happen concerning perception, so that what has a slight resemblance appears to be that thing. For when he sleeps, as the pneuma and the blood go down to the starting point, there go down with them also the motions and impressions of the perceptibles present in them as in a substrate, some potentially, some actually, that is, some about to [come] and not yet, others present and moving the perceptive starting point to apprehension, so that it happens that, in the motion that entered first, this one which will be active after it comes to the surface, and when that has perished, the next enters. And they are related to one another like the moulded frogs that rise in water as the salt dissolves. For suppose someone placed wooden frogs, say five in number, into a jar filled with salt, set from top to bottom and at intervals, so that of the extremes one lies by the rim and the other at the bottom, and the middle ones in proportion, all of them hidden; then, if the salt begins to dissolve from the top, the topmost frog of all will first come to the surface of the water and become actually perceptible, then, as the dissolving proceeds, the one after it, and after that one the next, and last of all, when the salt has dissolved, the lowest will come up. So too the motions in sleep and the semblances of the perceptibles: those that come up first will also be active first, while those that are potential will be active later, when at some point the hindering blood is relaxed and released, and further when what remains is thinned and purified, | more precisely. Hence the last parts of sleep give truer dreams, and at that time the likenesses of the perceptibles in the sense organs strike the starting point more purely, since what disturbs has by then come to rest. The change of images in dreams, then, resembles that in clouds, as was said before, which people liken to men and centaurs as they change rapidly. In general, each of the things that appear in sleep is a remnant, as was said at the beginning, of the actual sensation; and when the true perceptible has gone, if the judging [faculty] is not held fast by the blood that has gone down, it is true for one sleeping to say: this is not Coriscus, but like Coriscus and a semblance; and through this he thinks of the true Coriscus. But when it is completely held fast, so that the likeness and the semblance seem to be the true thing itself, it is not moved by the semblances as a perceiving and in a way waking [faculty], but as an unperceiving one; and so great is the power of sleep that it makes this escape notice. So, just as, if the finger pressed under the eye ever escapes notice, the one thing will not only appear but will also be believed to be two, whereas when it does not escape notice, it will appear so but not be believed, so too in sleep: if one perceives that one is asleep and, in addition, [is aware] of the dream, it will appear, but something in him says that this image appears to be Coriscus, yet is not (for often someone who is asleep and aware of it says in his soul that what appears is a dream); but if it escapes him that he is asleep, he will assent and will in no way contradict the imagination.

That what we say is true, and that there are imaginative motions and impressions and semblances of perceptibles in the primary sense organ, the heart, even when the things are not present and the senses are at rest, the [motions] around which the whole stage-production of dreams is composed, is clear from the following. For what is in the secondary [organs] is much more in the primary; and if there are semblances and residues in the other sense organs even when they are not active, much more are they in the heart, from which these [organs] have both their being and their activity. That they exist is evident if one attentively tries to remember what we undergo when waking up, when the waking happens close to the falling asleep. For sometimes on waking he will catch the semblances that appeared to him while asleep as being motions in the sense organs; for if someone who is drowsing begins to see a dream and is at once woken, he sees semblances before his eyes. For to some of the younger people, even when they are looking quite precisely, if it is dark, many moving semblances appear, so that they often cover their heads in fear. These were the motions in the eyes arising from the perceptibles. From all these things, then, one must conclude that the dream is an image in sleep, when the authoritative and judging [faculty] is held fast. So neither are the semblances and images mentioned dreams, nor anything else that appears when the senses are released and active, nor is every image in sleep [a dream], unless the mind lies asleep along with [the senses], not judging what is seen. And what happens to some, that they somehow perceive sounds and flavours and light and touch, though feebly and as if from far off, is not a dream. For those who are drowsing and are between the simply waking and the sleeping, if someone makes a noise or passes by holding a light, perceive both the light and the noises, but think they perceive them in a dream, so that many, when woken, say to them: 'You are making a noise' or 'You are holding the light; by the sun, I thought I was seeing these things in a dream', whereas perhaps it was not a dream but true. For as the simply waking stands to the one waking in a way, so too simple perception stands to perception in a way. These people, at any rate, often while sleeping, with their eyelids not shut but gently and slightly open, seeing the light of the lamp lying nearby and thinking it a dream, on being woken at once recognised it as being the lamp's; and hearing faintly the voice of cocks and dogs and supposing them to be dreams, on waking recognised clearly that they were not. Some even answer when questioned, often, but on waking do not remember that they answered. And it is clear that they were neither simply awake (for then they would have remembered) nor wholly asleep (for they would not have answered). None of the things mentioned, then, is to be called a dream, nor indeed the true thoughts that occur in sleep beside the images (I mean the judgements by which, while dreaming, we are aware that we are dreaming); rather the image arising from the motion of the sense-impressions, when it is in sleeping and insofar as one sleeps, this is a dream. It has already happened to some that they have seen no dream in their whole life, and to others that, when well advanced in age, they saw [one] though they had not seen [any] before. | The cause of its not happening before appears similar to the case of children and of [sleep] after food; for those whose nature is so constituted that much exhalation is carried up to the upper region, which, coming down, produces a mass of motion, to them, reasonably, no image appears; but as age advances it is nothing strange for a dream to appear; for when some change occurs, either through age or through an affection, this reversal must happen.
ON DIVINATION IN SLEEP.

As for the divination that occurs in sleep and is said to come about from dreams, it is neither easy to despise it nor to be persuaded of it. For the fact that all or many suppose dreams to have something significant and to be a foreshadowing of things to come gives credibility, as being said from experience; for it persuades us that what happens on each occasion is significant. And that there is divination in dreams about some things is not incredible; for it has some reason; one might almost suppose that all dreams have something significant. But the fact of seeing no reasonable cause by which it might come about makes one disbelieve. For [to say] that it is god who sends them, besides its other unreasonableness, it is also unreasonable that he sends them not to the best and wisest but to anyone at all. And when the cause from god is removed, none of the other causes appears reasonable; for that someone should foresee things at the Pillars of Heracles or on the Borysthenes would seem to be beyond our understanding to find the starting point of. Necessarily, then, dreams are either causes or signs | of what comes about, or coincidences; either all of these or some, or one only. I call a cause, for instance, the moon of the sun's eclipse, and fatigue of fever; a sign of the eclipse, the star's entering and running under, and roughness of the tongue of having a fever; and a coincidence, the sun's being eclipsed while one is walking; for my walking is neither a sign nor a cause of the eclipse. Hence coincidences happen neither always nor for the most part. Accordingly, of dreams some are signs, some causes, some coincidences; signs are those through which bodily or mental affections are presented and shown in advance; for the accomplished among physicians too say that one must pay close attention to dreams, since in them it will be possible to infer about the coming illness. It is reasonable to suppose so both for practitioners and for those who inquire and philosophise about something. For the motions that occur by day, unless they are very great and strong, escape notice beside the greater waking ones. In sleeping the whole is the reverse; for even small ones seem to be great. This is clear from what happens to many often; for they think they are struck by thunderbolts and thunder when small sounds occur in the ears, and that they enjoy honey and sweet flavours when a tiny bit of phlegm trickles down, and that they walk through fire and are heated intensely when a very slight warmth occurs about some parts. When they wake, these things are found to be thus. So, since the starting points of all things are small, clearly so too are those of the illnesses and other affections | that are going to arise in bodies. It is evident, then, that these must be more manifest in sleep than in waking.

But of what, and how, dreams are signs has been said; how they are also causes, and of what, will now be stated. That [they are causes] of each person's own actions and not of others' would seem more reasonable. For just as, when we are about to do something, or are in the midst of actions, or have done them, we often by a direct dream are occupied with them and act from the starting points of the day, so in turn the motions in sleep must often be a starting point of actions by day, because the mind is paved in advance toward these too in the nocturnal visions. In this way, then, it is possible for some dreams to be both signs and causes; but most resemble coincidences, especially all the extravagant ones and those whose starting point is not in [the dreamers] themselves, for instance about a sea-battle taking place in Persia and other things happening far away. For about these it is likely to be the same as when, while someone is mentioning something, this happens to come about. For what prevents it from being so in sleep too? Rather, it is likely that these things happen [so]. So, just as mentioning someone is neither a sign nor a cause of his arriving, so neither there, after the dream has appeared, is it in truth either a sign or a cause, but a coincidence. That is why many dreams do not come true; for coincidences happen neither always nor for the most part.

And in general, since some of the other animals too dream, | dreams would not be sent by god, nor have they come about for this purpose; they are, however, daimonic; for nature is daimonic, not divine. A sign: quite worthless people are foresighted and have direct dreams, as though god were not sending them, but those whose nature is, as it were, talkative and melancholic, seeing visions of every kind; and because they are moved by many and varied things, they hit the mark, just as some, when competing, snatch not one but many [prizes], if many things are thrown; and as it is said, 'if you throw many times, you will throw now this, now that', so this happens in these cases too. That many dreams do not come true is nothing strange; for neither do many signs in bodies and in the heavens, such as those of rains and winds; for if another motion more authoritative than this one occurs, from which, as it was impending, the sign arose, [the event] does not happen. For someone who saw in sleep that he was going through mire fell ill by day (for when the putrefied humours within began to move during the night, he, being at rest, gained perception [of them]), and [another saw himself] crossing over fire, and shortly after had a fever. But at another time, seeing these things, he did not fall ill, because his nature, roused and having concocted the humours, barred entry to the affection. And we take the halo around the moon as a token of rain and winds, but often when it forms none of these happens, because of the counter-displacement, the surrounding [air] being overpowered by the opposite motion. And many things well planned among what ought to be done have been dissolved because of other more authoritative starting points. For in general not everything that was going to be comes about, nor is what will be the same as what is going to be; but nevertheless | one must say that there were starting points from which [things] were not accomplished, and these are by nature signs of certain things that do not come about.

As for dreams that do not have such starting points, nor concern things over which we have control, but things beyond our bounds in time or place or magnitude, or even things done nearby, perhaps at a neighbour's, yet not having their starting points in those who saw the dream: if the foreseeing does not come about by coincidence, it would be otherwise rather than as Democritus says. For he gives as the cause semblances and effluences, some of which, he says, do good and others harm; they are of enormous size and hard to destroy, and they approach human beings and foretell what is to come when they are seen, sometimes also uttering voices perceptible only in sleep to those who hear them; hence he even prays to meet with fortunate semblances. But we altogether reject talk of semblances travelling, and introduce instead certain motions from the starting points of words and deeds that are going to happen; by these the air is shaped, and when they strike the heart in sleep through the ears or the nostrils, [one] foresees what is to come. For just as, when something moves water or air, this moves another thing, and when the first has stopped it happens that the same motion goes on up to a point though the mover is not present, so nothing prevents some motion and perception from reaching the dreaming souls, from the things out of which he makes his semblances and effluences, and, wherever they happen to arrive, from being more perceptible by night, because travelling by day they are dissolved more (for the air is less turbulent at night, since nights are calmer), and from producing perception in the body because of sleep; for we perceive small motions more when asleep than when awake. So when the perceptions mentioned produce appearances in the ruling part, the foreseeing comes about; and for this reason this affection happens to ordinary people and not to the wise. For it would also occur by day, and to the wise, if it were a god who sent it. And further, if foreseeing comes about in this way, it is likely that ordinary people foresee more; for the mind of such people is not given to thought, but is as it were deserted and empty of all the things with which the mind of those who philosophise is full, and when moved it is led along by what moves it. And the cause of some deranged people foreseeing is that their own motions do not disturb them but are beaten back. So they perceive most of all the foreign motions and those that strike from outside. That some people have direct dreams especially about those they know, and foresee [about them], happens because acquaintances think most about one another; for just as they recognise and perceive them most quickly by sight when they are far off, so too with the impressions and motions in the heart. For the motions of acquaintances are more familiar. Melancholics, because of the vehemence [of their motion], like those who shoot hard and hit with the arrow, even from far off, what others reach by hand, these too as it were snatch in advance what is to come by the speed of their motion; for since their imaginative [part] is easily changed, it quickly imagines what follows on the starting point of what will be. For just as people recite and string together the poems of Philaegides, which have no shifts of characters or narratives but always keep to what is alike (for instance, if he spoke of Aphrodite at the beginning, he keeps to her until the end), so too the frenzied think and see things that keep to what is alike. And besides this, because of its vehemence their motion is not knocked out by another motion. The most skilful interpreter of dreams is he who is able to discern the likenesses; for to interpret direct dreams is anyone's [task]; I mean the likenesses, because the appearances turn out similar to the images in water, as has also been said before. For there, if the water is not still but much motion arises, the reflection and the images do not come out like the real things; and in sleep, when the back-flow carried down toward the heart happens to be violent and confused, it allows neither like nor clear impressions and residues to be imagined. For the motion cuts off direct dreams. Each, then, will be a clever interpreter: the one who can discern the reflections and quickly perceive in disturbed water, and refer the shifted and distorted images to the real things, for instance that this is [the image] of a man or of a horse, even though such a thing was not seen [clearly], and the one who can do this very thing in sleep. What sleep and dream are, then, and for what cause each of them comes about, and further about divination from dreams, has been stated; now we must speak about the common motion of animals.
